findings.description: Shell command execution via pty.spawn with user-influenced arguments (sys.argv[1:])
findings.reasoning: The code at line 229 in rich/ansi.py calls pty.spawn with sys.argv[1:] as the command and arguments. This means any user input provided as command-line arguments will be executed as a shell command. If an attacker can control the arguments to this script, they can execute arbitrary commands, leading to a command injection vulnerability. There is no sanitization or validation of sys.argv[1:] before passing it to pty.spawn.

evidence.full_context:
decoder = AnsiDecoder()

    stdout = io.BytesIO()

    def read(fd: int) -> bytes:
        data = os.read(fd, 1024)
        stdout.write(data)
        return data

    pty.spawn(sys.argv[1:], read)

    from .console import Console

    console = Console(record=True)

    stdout_result = stdout.getvalue().decode("utf-8")
    print(stdout_result)

    for line in decoder.decode(stdout_result):
        console.print(line)

findings.description: Shell command execution via pty.spawn with sys.argv[1:] as command, potentially allowing arbitrary command execution if arguments are influenced by untrusted input.
findings.reasoning: The code at line 229 in rich/ansi.py invokes pty.spawn with sys.argv[1:] as the command argument. This means any arguments passed to the script (except the script name itself) are directly used as the command to execute in a new pseudo-terminal. If an attacker can control the command-line arguments, they can execute arbitrary shell commands, leading to command injection (CWE-78). There is no sanitization or validation of sys.argv[1:] before use, making this a high-severity vulnerability.
